newsitem.title: ZAIRE: U.N. aid train attacked in eastern Zaire.
newsitem.headline: U.N. aid train attacked in eastern Zaire.

text.p: Zaireans attacked a train loaded with food in eastern Zaire in protests against aid for Rwandan refugees on Monday, forcing the suspension of U.N. operations, witnesses said.
A foreign journalist said Zaireans were on the rampage south of Kisangani and had shown her the bodies of six people they said were killed by Rwandan Hutu militiamen among the refugees.
"The residents were going crazy, waving sticks, clubs and hunting knives," said the journalist, adding that she was attacked.
U.N. aid agencies suspended operations south of Kisangani due to the renewed unrest by residents angry at the presence of an estimated 100,000 Rwandan refugees and the aid they are being given.
U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) spokeswoman Brenda Barton said a WFP storekeeper 25 km (15 miles) south of Kisangani heard shooting at 3 a.m. on Monday and saw local people looting a warehouse.
He fled to Kisangani. It was not immediately known how much food was taken or exactly who was responsible for the shooting.

Barton said the aid train loaded with 120 tonnes of food left Kisangani at 7 p.m. (1700 GMT) on Sunday after receiving permission from rebel authorities but was stopped seven km (four miles) south of the city by rebels citing insecurity ahead.

"At 4 a.m. the (rebel) military said it could proceed. Two WFP Zairean staff on the train then said people suddenly appeared out of the forest and violently attacked the train and they were forced to flee on foot," she said.
"The two staff arrived back in Kisangani this morning. We have no confirmation the train was looted but we assume it was either partially or totally looted by the local population," she said.
WFP staff said residents surrounded the aid train despite rebel guards shooting in the air to keep them back.
Barton said rebel authorities had barred foreign aid workers from travelling from Kisangani to the camps on Monday so WFP staff had not gone down to assess what happened to the train.

She said the 120 tonnes of maize meal, pulses, vegetable oil and corn soya blend was intended for 32,000 Rwandan refugees at a makeshift camp at Biaro, 42 km (25 miles) south of Kisangani, and smaller groups at km 82 (50 miles) and farther south.
"We are seeing a pattern of problems. Our staff could not move to the camps on Friday, our warehouse in Kisangani was looted and now food has been looted from the train," she said.
"Definitely we will want security guarantees," said Barton, adding the 120 tonnes was equivalent to one day of heavy airlifting of supplies to Kisangani, capital of northeast Zaire.
Yagi Sitolo, governor of Eastern Province, said in Kisangani on Sunday a planned U.N. airlift of an estimated 100,000 refugees should not start until May 5 due to a cholera epidemic.

He intervened last week to delay the start of the airlift from Friday because of the cholera outbreak before attacks on aid workers by residents angry at the amount of aid being given to the refugees.
The death toll from cholera, malaria and malnutrition among the refugees stands at about 40 a day, with bodies lined up under blankets along a mud road leading through the camps.
Local residents stopped aid workers reaching the camps south of Kisangani on Friday and looted 15 tonnes of food from WFP.

Angry local people broke the windscreen of a U.N. vehicle returning from the camps on Saturday. Privately, aid workers say they fear the protests are orchestrated by the rebels, who deny any involvement.
